reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / ACR-EULAR
clinicalPearls: A necrotising vasculitis of medium-sized muscular arteries that characteristically spares the lungs and is not associated with ANCA
Presents with systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss, malaise) plus organ-specific ischaemic damage
Peripheral nervous system involvement, especially mononeuritis multiplex, is common and an important clue
Skin manifestations include livedo reticularis, tender nodules, ulcers, and digital ischaemia
Renal involvement is typically renovascular ischaemia and hypertension rather than glomerulonephritis, and gut involvement can cause mesenteric ischaemia and abdominal pain
A recognised association with hepatitis B infection exists, so viral serology should be checked
Diagnosis rests on biopsy of affected tissue showing necrotising arteritis, or angiography demonstrating microaneurysms and stenoses in visceral vessels
Treatment uses corticosteroids with additional immunosuppression for severe disease, while hepatitis B-associated cases also require antiviral therapy
reference.pathophysiology: Polyarteritis nodosa is a systemic necrotising vasculitis affecting medium and small muscular arteries. Transmural inflammation with fibrinoid necrosis weakens the vessel wall, producing the microaneurysms characteristic of visceral angiography, while intimal proliferation and thrombosis cause luminal narrowing and downstream tissue infarction. Lesions are segmental and favour branch points. Unlike small-vessel vasculitides it does not typically involve capillaries, glomeruli, or the pulmonary circulation and is ANCA-negative. Immune complex mechanisms are implicated, particularly in hepatitis B-associated disease.
additionalDifferentials: ANCA-associated vasculitides (granulomatosis with polyangiitis, microscopic polyangiitis)
Fibromuscular dysplasia and segmental arterial mediolysis
additionalInvestigations: Visceral angiography (renal, mesenteric) for microaneurysms and stenoses
Biopsy of clinically involved tissue (e.g. nerve, muscle, skin) showing necrotising arteritis
Inflammatory markers, renal function, and urinalysis (typically without active urinary sediment)
Nerve conduction studies for mononeuritis multiplex and ANCA testing (expected negative)
redFlags: Acute abdomen from mesenteric ischaemia, bowel infarction, or perforation
Rapidly progressive renal impairment or malignant hypertension from renal artery involvement
Cardiac ischaemia or heart failure from coronary arteritis
New neurological deficit including stroke or severe mononeuritis multiplex
reference.prognosis: Untreated disease has a poor outlook, but immunosuppression markedly improves survival. Prognosis is worse with significant gastrointestinal, renal, cardiac, or central nervous system involvement; hepatitis B-associated disease can respond well when the virus is also treated.
pitfalls: Confusing it with ANCA-associated vasculitis and expecting lung or glomerular disease
Failing to test for hepatitis B, which alters management
Missing mesenteric ischaemia in a patient with vague abdominal pain
Overlooking mononeuritis multiplex as a diagnostic clue
Delaying tissue or angiographic confirmation in a critically ill patient
management: Induction immunosuppression with high-dose corticosteroids plus cyclophosphamide for organ- or life-threatening disease
For hepatitis B-associated disease, combine antiviral therapy with a short course of corticosteroids and plasma exchange rather than prolonged immunosuppression
Maintenance immunosuppression such as azathioprine with corticosteroid tapering once remission is achieved in idiopathic disease
Corticosteroids alone may suffice for milder disease without critical organ involvement
Supportive care with analgesia, blood pressure control for renovascular hypertension, and neuropathic pain management for mononeuritis multiplex
Monitor disease activity, organ function and treatment toxicity, with vigilance for relapse and infection prophylaxis
Rheumatology-led multidisciplinary care with nephrology, neurology and gastroenterology input as involvement dictates
Escalate for mesenteric ischaemia, gastrointestinal, cardiac or central nervous system involvement
